\+ The best story of the summer so far is Trump fleeing the NATO summit in a
catering cart….The great American bully sneaking away in a white van filled
with cupcakes, eclairs, and macarons, as his Qatari-gifted luxury jet sat on
the tarmac, deemed too easy a target for Iranian missiles that Pistol Pete
Hegseth had supposedly bombed out of existence, is an image that will stay
with me for a long time. I hope Trump didn't forget, as Clemenza admonished
Michael Corleone in The Godfather, to "take the cannoli" home to the ever-
adulatory Natalie Harp, his Human Printer. But, alas, fearing for his life, he
probably did.

confidence](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/08/12/cia-
had-low-confidence-iranian-threat-before-trump-switched-planes-turkey/) in the

pastry van. Well, he didn’t run so much as lurched, perhaps in a [leg
brace](https://www.irishstar.com/news/us-news/donald-trump-stance-leg-
brace-37533990).

\+ The French novelist Honoré de Balzac hid from his creditors for nearly
seven years on the top floor of a house on the Rue Berton in the Passy
district of Paris, keeping his location secret from nearly everyone except his
mistress, the Polish countess, Madame (Ewelina) Henska. He could rarely
venture outside because his Balzacian girth made him instantly recognizable to
the bailiffs who were looking to arrest him and toss him into debtor’s prison.
So he wrote and he wrote, his swelling body swaddled in a monk-like white
cashmere hooded gown and fueled by 50 cups of coffee a day

In a letter to Henska he described his writing routine: “Working, dear
Countess, is to get up every night at 12, write until 8, take breakfast for a
quarter of an hour, then work until 5, dine, go to sleep, wake up at midnight
and start all over again.” In his seven years in the house, he wrote the
novels: The Black Sheep, Cousin Bette, A Murky Business, Cousin Pons and Lost
Illusions. Not bad for a hedonist.

If you’re lying in bed at Fitzgerald’s witching hour (3 am, unable to get back
to sleep (nearly every night for me these days) you might try another book
Balzac wrote in his secret garret, the novella _Sarrasine,_ about a young
French sculptor who goes to Rome to become the next Michelangelo and falls
madly in love with a singer who turns out to be a castrato.

In Balzac’s story, Sarrasine attends the opera one night and becomes obsessed
with the beauty of one of the singers, who goes by the flamboyant stage name
La Zambinella. Sarrasine rushes back to his studio and, in a lustful frenzy,
begins molding a clay statue of the singer, viewing her as the very model of
modern femininity. He attends the same play over and over again and ultimately
tries to seduce her, but she resists his advances without offering a
convincing explanation.

Finally, he plots to abduct her during an appearance at the French embassy in
Rome, where La Zambinella appears dressed in men’s clothing. Surprised, but
intrigued by her appearance, Sarrasine is told that Zambinella is not a young
woman, but a male castrato, whose testicles had been hacked off as a young
teen to sustain the soprano registers of his voice.

Humiliated and enraged, Sarrasine grabs Zambinella and drags “her” to his
studio, where he plans to kill the object of his desire, only to discover, too
late, that he/she has other admirers, less unnerved by her transgendered
nature, including a cardinal of the Church, who has sent his agents to stab
Sarrasine to death before he can slit Zambinella’s throat. The whole story is
pretty far-out, particularly for 1830.

The novella formed part of Balzac’s _La Comédie humaine_ series but had been
suppressed for obvious reasons until 1970, when Roland Barthes took it apart
almost sentence by sentence in his book _S/Z._ The Barthes book is barely
readable, but Balzac roars along as immediate as ever and nearly 200 years
later almost perfectly captures the gender hysteria of our time. The Crying
Game has nothing on this story.

\+ In 1948, Belgian literary scholar Paul de Man arrived in New York City,
where he quickly ingratiated himself with Manhattan’s literary circle,
including the socialist Dwight Macdonald, former editor of the Partisan Review
(and movie critic for the Today Show!) and novelist Mary McCarthy, with whom
he likely had an affair. De Man cultivated the image of a Resistance fighter;
along with what Harold Bloom called his Apollo-like looks, that persona helped
propel him to the heights of literary theory, with posts at Harvard, Cornell,
and Yale and a lifelong friendship with Jacques Derrida. In essence, de Man’s
theory held that searching for meaning in literature is futile: there’s
nothing but the text and the text means nothing. So it's not for nothing (or
perhaps it is for "nothing") that his Yale colleague Geoffrey Hartman called
de Man “the connoisseur of nothingness.”

Yet de Man, who became a celebrity professor at Yale and one of the world’s
most-cited post-structuralist thinkers, was hiding a secret that may help
explain his insistence that written works have no fixed meaning. Far from
fighting in the Belgian or French Resistance, de Man had written more than 100
columns for the Nazi-controlled Belgian newspaper _Le Soir_ —a fact he
concealed until 1987, three years after his death from cancer.

In one of those historical synchronicities that would have thrilled Carl Jung,
an early devotee of Paul de Man was none other than Henry Kissinger, who a few
years later would leave his own trail of nothingness from Southeast Asia to
South America. In the early 1950s, Kissinger hired de Man as his private
French tutor and was quickly dazzled by the Belgian savant’s wide-ranging, if
nihilistic, intellect. Kissinger may not have known that de Man had written
for a pro-Nazi, antisemitic publication. But as a self-proclaimed sage of
postwar European history, he was almost certainly aware that de Man’s uncle,
Hendrik de Man, was a Nazi collaborator who served as the Hitler-approved
prime minister of Belgium during the occupation.
